en: *The Outline of the Text and Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one fascicle.
Now, as for the vast ocean of nature (*dharmatā*), how can its source be fathomed through conditioned phenomena?

As for the profound and mysterious Way, its limits are rarely found through names and words. There is the harmonious, perfect wisdom that illuminates the great night and dispels the heavy darkness; without it—
Constrained by great compassion, he looks down upon the various capacities of sentient beings and approaches the myriad lands.
Thus, though formless, he manifests form, like the rising sun from the eastern valley;
though wordless, he reveals words, like the vast waves pouring into a great abyss.
Therefore, originating within the Lotus Treasury World, it unfolds the inexhaustible profound framework;
it encompasses those of the highest attainment and guides them beyond the surface of the spiritual fountain.

Thereafter, transformation moistens the Sahā world as the clouds of compassion gradually spread; they sprinkle a subtle dew to nourish the three faculties and foster the sprouts of the Way so that all return to the single source.
Thus we know that because the conditions of sentient beings differ, the responses of the Sage are accordingly distinguished;
yet though these responses differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the magnificent discourse gathered from the ocean-like assembly and the ultimate teaching that illuminates the King of Mountains. Its principles are vast and profound, extending throughout the entire dharma-realm to the very source of truth;
its boundless subtle words pervade the void like space and reach into every land.
Thus, without deficiency regarding the large or the small, the vast and immense lands enter the tip of a single hair;
without difficulty regarding the great or the minute, the ultimate atom merges with the entirety of space.

Therefore, the Indra’s net reflects one another in layered interdependence, and the crystal-like radiance of Dīpaṃkara shines faintly across every direction of the dust-motes. The one is many without obstruction, and the many are one in perfect penetration; the nine periods of time are subsumed within a single kṣaṇa, and a single thought-moment is extended to encompass eternal kalpas.
The three births are consummated, with the firm seed serving as the cause;
the ten stages of faith reach their perfection, with universal virtues manifesting as the fruit.
The fruit is no different from the fruit of its cause; thus the five positions are distinguished to mark their respective paths.
Because there is no cause that does not produce its corresponding fruit, the ten bodies are unified in their ultimate realization.
Therefore, the Mother of Awakening (Prajñāpāramitā) appeared before sentient beings in the Eastern City, where six thousand commentaries elucidated her ten eyes;
and the Youth (Mañjuśrī) consulted his friends in the Southern Land, where one hundred and ten [treatises] were completed within a single lifetime.
Thus, without the King of Trees (the Bodhi tree) being moved, the six heavens were reached;
how could the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka Sūtra) be shifted, for the ten lands are empty and harmonious?
Within the dust, he revealed the precious verses, their brilliance equaling that of the eight assemblies.
The jade-like pearls of inherent virtue are revealed, perfectly manifesting in seven locations.
Vast and resonant, they transcend thought and soar far beyond;
towering and brilliantly radiant, they isolate the deaf and blind from ordinary sight and hearing.
Therefore, when Śākyamuni first fashioned [the Dharma] through the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, it first arose on the morning of the fourteenth day;
when Nāgārjuna finally looked down from the palace of the dragon-kings, it was only after six hundred years that it became manifest.

Thus, "Great" (Mahā-) takes embracing and containing as its meaning; "Square" (Pra-) takes providing a model and standard as its function; "Broad" (Vi-) signifies that the essence is ultimate and the application is all-pervasive; "Buddha" (Buddha) refers to the fruit being perfected and enlightenment being full; "Flower" (Puṣpa) is a metaphor for the blossoming of the myriad practices; "Adornment" (Sūtra) is an analogy for embellishing this fundamental essence; and "Sūtra" (Sūtra) means to string together and stitch, wherein the teaching capable of expression is manifested.
Proceeding from the Dharma to the person, this title is established by means of metaphorical designation; thus it is called the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding the "Chapter on the World’s Pure Eye": just as the three types of vessels and so forth shine forth at that time, so too does the pure eye illuminate with brilliant clarity.
Because the Dharma and its analogy are presented together, it is called "The World’s Pure Eye.
Since language and principle correspond and categories follow one another, it is termed a "Chapter" (*parivarta*).

This sutra contains thirty-four chapters; as this chapter stands at the beginning, it is called the "First. Thus, it is titled: *The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter One: The World’s Pure Eye*.
The remaining meanings are as explained below.
Now, summarizing the distinctions in the events and meanings of this sutra across its seven locations and eight assemblies, ten general gates are briefly opened:

first, identifying the causes for the arising of the teaching; second, explaining the title of the sutra; third, clarifying the essential purport of the sutra; fourth, stating the time and place of the discourse; fifth, identifying the primary teacher; sixth, clarifying the distinctions in the number of the assembly; seventh, defining the scope of the request for the teaching; eighth, the samādhis entered; ninth, the empowerment of the Buddha’s light; and tenth, the formal exposition of the chapters and assemblies.
Regarding the causes for the initial emergence of the teaching, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the characteristics of the transmission of the teaching; second, discerning the intent behind the emergence of the teaching.

First, concerning the characteristics of the transmission of the teaching: according to tradition from the Western Regions, after this sutra was compiled, it was deposited within the Dragon Palace. Six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna went to the Dragon Palace and beheld this Great Inconceivable Sutra. Its superior version contained verses as numerous as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and chapters as numerous as the atoms in the four continents.
The middle version consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses in one thousand two hundred chapters;
the shorter version consists of one hundred thousand verses in thirty-eight chapters.

Nāgārjuna subsequently took this lower version of the text and brought it to the kingdom of India, where he composed the *Acintyastava* (Treatise on the Inconceivable) in one hundred thousand verses to explain this sūtra.
The *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* translated today by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra is but one chapter of that work.

There was a śramaṇa from the Eastern Jin dynasty named Zhi Falin, who obtained these thirty-six thousand gāthās from the kingdom of Khotan. He also invited the Mahāyāna third-stage bodhisattva meditation master named Buddhabhadra—translated as "Jue Xian" (Awakened Virtue)—whose secular surname was Śākya and who was a descendant of King Amṛtodana, to come to the Jin court.

On the tenth day of the third month of the year of the Bird-Fire (Chun-huo), the fourteenth year of Emperor An’s Yixi era, he separately constructed a Huajing Huayan Dharma Hall at Xie Sikong Temple in Yangzhou, wherein he translated this sutra.

At that time, there was a lotus pond in front of the hall; every day two youths dressed in green emerged from the pond, swept and sprinkled the area, and ground ink, returning to the pond at dusk. They continued this until the sutra was finished, at which point they ceased.
The tradition explains that because this sutra had long remained in the Dragon Palace, the Dragon King was made to serve as an attendant out of celebration for its transmission to the human realm.
Later, the name of this monastery was changed to Xingyan Temple (Temple of Flourishing Adornment).

There were the Śramaṇas of the Jin dynasty, Shi Faye, Huiyan, Huiguan, and others, who personally received the teachings from the brush of [Tanyue]. Consequently, Faye produced a commentary on the meaning entitled *Huayan Zhiguī* (The Essential Return of the Avataṃsaka), in two fascicles.
The patrons (dānapati) included Meng Yi, Governor of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard.

The translation was completed on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Yuanxi era. It was further collated against the Sanskrit original on the twentieth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yongchu era of the Dazong reign, at which time it consisted of fifty fascicles.
Later, there was also a version compiled by Rong in sixty fascicles, which already lacked eight or nine sheets of text within the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" chapter.

Now, in the third month of the first year of the Yonglong era of the Great Tang, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India, Śīlabhadra (translated into Chinese as Rìzhào), by imperial decree, together with the śramaṇa Daocheng and ten other eminent virtuous ones, translated and supplemented this text at Taoyuan Monastery in the Western Capital; the śramaṇa Fuli acted as the scribe for the oral transmission.
Regarding the miraculous responses of this scripture and the spiritual traces of Buddhabhadra, these have all been examined in detail within the *New Collection of Avataṃsaka Biographies*.

Second, to clarify the intent behind the emergence of the teaching: the emergence of the Great Teaching does not occur without causes and conditions, nor does it arise through minor causes and conditions. Therefore, the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*) in the text below states: "By means of causes and conditions such as the atoms of Mount Sumeru, this Wheel of Dharma of the Arising of Nature is brought forth."

Now, ten types are briefly enumerated: namely, by reason of the power of vows; by reason of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); as the basis; as the refuge; for the purpose of manifesting virtues; for the purpose of manifesting stages; for the purpose of development; by means of seeing and hearing; for the purpose of accomplishing practice; and for the purpose of attaining the fruit.

Regarding "firstly, by the power of the original vow," this refers to that which is initiated by the power of the vows of three positions: the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, and the corresponding capacity of the recipient.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "By the power of the original vow of Vairocana Buddha, and by the power of the vow of Samantabhadra."
It is further said: "If there are those who hear [this], you should know it is due to the power of the original vow.
It is also said: "Because it develops the great vow, it emerges from the power of the original vow."

Regarding "the second reason being due to the nature of things (*dharmatā*)," this means that whenever a Buddha first appears in the world and intends to reveal and clarify the lotus-like phenomena for those to be converted, it is the very nature of things that, during the second seven-day period, he shall manifest such inexhaustible dharma-gates from within the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
The subsequent text states: "Because the Dharma is thus, this is like the royal highway—the eternal norm of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the root": this means that when one intends to gradually bestow the secondary teachings according to the capacities of beings, one first demonstrates this Dharma at the outset to serve as the root of those secondary teachings, for it is by relying on this root that the secondary teachings can arise.
The subsequent text states: "For example, the pure dharma-realm serves as the basis for the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
It further states: "Just as when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains," and so forth.
"Fourth, for the sake of the ultimate refuge" means to reveal the destination to which the provisional teachings ultimately lead.
As the subsequent text states: "Just as all waters flow back to the great ocean," and so forth.
Regarding the fifth point, "to manifest the virtues," this means to manifest the essence, characteristics, and functions of the Dharma-body attained by the Tathāgata himself.

"Essence" refers to the non-obstruction between the Dharma-realm and wisdom; "characteristics" refers to the ten lotus-treasury worlds, as numerous as atoms; and "function" refers to the manifestation of buddha-lands from every pore to extensively benefit sentient beings according to their capacities—Puxian Bodhisattva is likewise so.

Regarding "the sixth, because it reveals the stages": this means that it reveals how the six stages—faith and the others—are perfectly interfused and mutually inclusive throughout their sequence; therefore, a single stage is all stages, yet the preceding and succeeding stages remain distinct and clear.
The subsequent text states: "Abiding in the first stage, one universally encompasses the merits of all stages," and so forth.

Regarding the seventh point, "because of development," this refers to developing the dharma-gate of the unimpeded mastery of the *dharmadhātu* within the *tathāgatagarbha* (the nature-arising mind) of sentient beings, thereby causing it to manifest.
This can be understood from the passage in the text below that reads, "breaking open a minute particle to reveal a sutra scroll," and so forth.

Regarding the eighth point, "because of seeing and hearing": this refers to demonstrating this single vehicle (ekayāna) as an inexhaustible, sovereign, and fully endowed dharma-gate of mutual support and non-obstruction, causing sentient beings to see and hear it so that they may establish the diamond-seed of the stage conducive to liberation.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*):

regarding the phrase "because it brings about the fulfillment of practice," this means causing sentient beings to accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra, wherein one single practice is all practices; at the very moment of first resolving for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening, fully endowed with the body of wisdom, and realizes this without depending on another.
Regarding "attaining the fruit through ten [aspects]," there are two parts.

First is the fruit of abandonment, which refers to the removal of hindrances; that is, the removal of one hindrance constitutes the removal of all hindrances, as explained in the "Chapter on Samantabhadra."
First is the severance of all through the severance of one, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics" (*Xiǎoxiàng pǐn*) and elsewhere.

Second is the fruit of wisdom, which refers to possessing the ten bodies, exhausting the three worlds, attaining mastery over both the direct and reverse orders of causality, and the non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants, and so forth.

By virtue of these ten meanings, which possess the power of being identical, dependently originated, unimpeded, perfectly interfused, and sovereign, this scriptural teaching is established upon the foundation of non-abiding.

Initially, based on the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, this scripture was titled the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
This name is derived from a metaphor, as it is a compilation formed through the intermingling of principle and practice within the process of dependent origination.
Second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on Entrustment," refers to this as the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra*, consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
This title is derived from the function of the Dharma; thus, the "Nature-Arising" chapter states: "This sūtra is established for Bodhisattvas who ride upon the inconceivable vehicle."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* itself refers to this sūtra.

Regarding the "one hundred thousand sūtras" mentioned in the tenth chapter on "Superior Characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Liang dynasty’s *Saṃgraha-bhāṣya*, it refers to the one hundred thousand verses of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
This is named according to its numerical value.

The four [types] are as described in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokātīta-parivarta*) regarding the production of the flowers of the profound and wondrous meaning of the bodhisattvas; that shall be explained there. Here, the name is applied by combining the dharma with the metaphor.
Fifth, regarding the establishment of names based on ten meanings, as in the "Nature-Arising" (Xingqi) Chapter, these shall also be explained when we reach that section.
Second, within the sub-section on the analysis of distinctions, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition.
Regarding "compendium" (vaipulya), as explained in the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra*, there are five meanings:

first, because it teaches remedial dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; second, because it contains many vehicles (yānas); third, because it possesses many ornaments; fourth, because it can produce immeasurable great fruits; and fifth, because it eliminates and severs all false views—it is therefore called vaipulya.

The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* explains that "Vaipulya" refers to the teachings associated with the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; it is called Vaipulya because it serves as the basis for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings and because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
It is also called "Extensive Destruction" because it can extensively destroy all obstacles;
it is also called "Incomparable" because there are no phenomena that can serve as its counterpart.
These are all distinct names for the Mahāyāna, due to its correspondence with the seven kinds of greatness, and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the separate explanation: "Mahāvaipulya" and so forth are the general names for this entire section, while "Worldly Pure Eye" is the specific title for this particular chapter.
Within the former [the general name], there are two parts:
first, the opening of the meaning; second, the combined explanation.
Regarding "Opening" (Kai): first, the meaning that is expressed (*vācya*) is presented;
subsequently, the single character "Sūtra" (Jing) presents the teaching that expresses it (*vācaka*). This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).
Within the former [section], first the object of comparison is clarified; subsequently, the two characters "Huayan" (Flower Ornament) are the means of comparison (*upamāna*).
In the preceding section, the first part clarifies the dharma upon which [the teaching] relies; the latter part, through the single character "Buddha" (佛), reveals the person who relies upon it.
Within the former, the first part specifically clarifies the essence and function; the latter part extensively analyzes the essence and capacity through the single character.
Within the former, the character "Da" (大) clarifies the essence of the dharma, while the character "Fang" (方) subsequently distinguishes its superior capacity.
In the combined explanation: "Great" (mahā) refers to its essential nature, with the meaning of "encompassing.
"Square" (vīthi) is named according to its function, with the meaning of "standard" or "model."
"Vast" (*vipula*) means that its essence and function are explained in conjunction, with "pervasive" as its primary meaning.
Here, "great" (*mahat*) is equivalent to "square" (*caturaśra*), and "vast great" (*vipulamahat*) is a *dharmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Furthermore, regarding "vast," the ancient masters explain that it possesses three meanings: [1] vastness of extent; [2] vastness of quality; and [3] vastness of inclusion.
First, the meaning of permanence.
The Sūtra says: "That which is called 'great' is termed 'permanent.
Second, the meaning of the universal pervasiveness of its essential nature.
The Sūtra says: "That which is called 'Great' has a nature that is vast and expansive.
This third point refers to the meaning of supreme capability.
The Sūtra says: "Because it can establish the great purpose, it is named Great Nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, it consists of the three greats: substance, characteristic, and function.
Now, seeking further according to the subsequent text, there are briefly ten meanings:
first, the greatness of the object (*viṣaya*).
Within this, there are two aspects:
first, the greatness of the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), which refers to the ten *padma-garbha* worlds;

second, the greatness of the primary retribution (*sambhoga-vipāka*), which refers to the three activities (*trikarma*) of the ten Buddhas and so forth, as explained in the "Śākyamuni" chapter and elsewhere—this is the object of faith.

Second is the greatness of mind, as explained at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (Bhadramukha-parivarta) and in the "Chapter on the Merits of Arousing the Mind" (Cittotpāda-guṇa-parivarta).
Third is the greatness of practice, as explained in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (Lokātīta-parivarta), which refers to the universal cultivation of practices throughout the six stages.

Regarding the four greatnesses, as explained from the "Chapter on Clarifying Difficulties" up to the sixth assembly, those five stages are taught: namely, the greatness of faith, the greatness of understanding, the greatness of practice, the greatness of aspiration, and the greatness of realization.

Fifth is the greatness of realization (*pratyakṣa-mahattva*), as explained in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) chapter, which refers to the common realization of the dharmas of the six stages.
Sixth is the greatness of causes (*hetu-mahattva*), which has two aspects:
first, the cause of production (*janana-hetu*), as described for the preceding five stages; [the second is the sustaining cause].
Second is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), as explained in the "Universal Worthy" chapter and others.
Seventh is the greatness of the fruit (*phala-mahattva*), which has two aspects:
first, the fruit that accords with conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartin-phala*), as explained in the "Inconceivable" chapter and others; [the second is the fruit of ultimate fulfillment].
Second is the fruit of its own essence (*svabhāva-phala*), which refers to that which cannot be expressed in the "Fruit Section" (*phalabhāga*) of this sutra.
Eighth is the greatness of its essence (*mahātmya-svabhāva*), as explained in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-parivarta*) and other texts.

Ninth is the greatness of function (*kārya-mahattva*), which refers to the continuous cultivation of benefit for sentient beings in every thought-moment, instantaneously perfecting the stages and so forth, as explained in the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics" (*Kṣudraka-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*) and elsewhere.
Tenth is the greatness of the Dharma (*dharma-mahattva*), which comprises three aspects:

first, the greatness of the teaching (*deśanā-mahattva*), meaning that each and every name and phrase pervades the entire ten-directional dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as stated in the following text.
Second is the greatness of meaning (*artha-mahattva*), which refers to the meanings manifested by the boundless teachings.
Third is the greatness of phenomena (*vastu-mahattva*), which means that each and every atom and so forth possesses all [phenomena].
These ten aforementioned meanings each comprehensively encompass all dharmas without exception; because they are fully present within each other, they are called "great."
The term "fang" (方) has three meanings:
first, the meaning of being upright and correct, which means that these ten meanings are by nature free from deviance and partiality;
second, the meaning of method, which means that these ten meanings all possess models and rules.
Third is the meaning of medical prescriptions (*cikitsā-vidhi*), which means that these ten meanings are all capable of counteracting various heavy obstacles.
"Extensive" has two meanings:

first, it pervades all places; this means that every single dharma-gate universally pervades all inexhaustible worlds, down to the paths of atoms and the locations of all other dharmas, as explained in the concluding passages on universal application and so forth.
Second, pervading all times, meaning it pervades the limits of the past and future, extending through the ten periods of time down to a single *kṣaṇa* and so forth.
This twofold [pervasion] has two types:
first, mutual interpenetration; second, layered interpenetration, such as that of Indra’s net and the like.
Although it is called "great" (*mahā*) because it encompasses all within one, and termed "vast" (*vipula*) because it pervades all,
there is no contradiction in also applying the former name "vast" to the latter and the latter name "great" to the former.
"Buddha" is named for its awakening and illumination, and its meaning is the fulfillment of the fruit; this applies to both the ten Buddhas and the three Buddhas.
"Vaipulya" (Extensive) refers to the Dharma attained, while "Buddha" refers to the person who attains it.
Furthermore, the former is the object of awakening, while the Buddha is the wisdom that awakens.
Within this context, there are two meanings regarding the relationship between the object and wisdom:
first, they are mutually constitutive; second, they are identical.
The "Vaipulya" (fangguǎng) of the former [category] distinguishes it from the Buddha-teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna).
The "Vaipulya" of the Buddha [himself] distinguishes it from the dharmas of the causal stage.
These two mutually complement one another; each possesses four propositions regarding the dependent origination of existence-nature and non-existence-nature, which should be contemplated accordingly.
The mutual dependence of person and dharma is explained according to the *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound).
As for the identity of the two aspects, sometimes the Vaipulya is identical to the Buddha, and the Buddha is identical to the Vaipulya, because there is no obstruction between person and dharma.
To cause the essence and its characteristics to be identical also involves four propositions; one should reflect upon this accordingly.
This is solely a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
The term "flower" (*puṣpa*) has three meanings:
First, the meaning of subtle excellence; second, the meaning of producing results; third, the meaning of adornment.
The first [meaning] illustrates the essence of practice, while the latter two illustrate the functions of practice.
Within these functions, the first illustrates the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), and the latter illustrates the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).

Furthermore, the first is the flower that produces fruit, which does not coexist with the fruit itself—just as the cycle of birth and death serves as the equipment for the Path, or as the roots of goodness in the stage of the cause.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "This sutra gives birth to the flowers of the profound and wondrous meanings of all the practices and merits of Bodhisattvas."
If one follows this principle, it should be called the "Vaipulya of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the subsequent "Adornment" (vyūha) refers to the flower that coexists with the fruit, like the roots of goodness at the stage of fruition.
Since this present text elucidates the Vaipulya of the Buddha, it discusses only the "Flower Adornment of the Buddha" from the perspective of the stage of fruition.
Furthermore, the first [of these three] is a subtle analogy for the preceding phenomenon (dharma), while the latter two are analogies for the person (pudgala).
Generally speaking, both persons and phenomena possess these three aspects; thus, they constitute a complete simile.
The single character "adornment" (yan) comprehensively encompasses both the agent of adornment and that which is adorned; through this integration, four propositions are formed.
Alternatively, the myriad practices may be the agent of adornment and true nature the object of adornment, because principle is manifested through cultivation.

Alternatively, the true nature is like the flower that serves as the adornment, while the various practices produced through cultivation serve as the ornament, because these practices arise from following the principle.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "There is nothing that does not flow forth from this dharmakāya, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this dharmakāya."
This is what is meant by that.

Alternatively, subject and object may both be fused, such that they are non-dual yet dual: for there can be no practice flowing from the Real to accord with the Real, nor can there be a practice that adorns the Real which does not arise from the Real.

It is because when the essence (*tǐ*) harmonizes with practice (*xíng*), the cause is perfected; and when practice encompasses the truth (*zhēn*), the fruit is fulfilled. For this reason, it is designated as the *Buddha-avataṃsaka*.

Alternatively, when subject and object are both extinguished, they are two yet non-dual. Since practice that is identical to truth is not practice, and truth that is identical to practice is not truth, then principle and practice are both transcended, and subject and object are both lost. Surpassing emotion and departing from form—this is called the *Avataṃsaka*.
The first two phrases mean "the adornment by means of flowers," while the latter two phrases mean "flowers are themselves the adornment"; these two interpretations may be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding the Flower Adornment of the Buddha of the Vaipulya [sūtras], both the sense of "adorned by flowers" and "flowers are themselves the adornment" may likewise be understood through these two interpretations.
The sūtra is explained as before.
"The world" (*loka*) refers to phenomena (*dharma*), while "pure eye" is the metaphor.
"World" (*loka*) means time, and "interval" (*antara*) means the midst; because it manifests within time, it is called the "world."
The world is diverse, and its meaning is threefold:
first, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), which has two aspects:
(1) distinct locations such as the grounds of practice; and...
Second, the common locus of the Lotus Treasury World;
second, the world of the Perfectly Enlightened One of Wisdom, which also has two aspects:
first, the three bodies (trikāya); second, the Buddhas.
The world of sentient beings also has two aspects:
first, those born together; second, those born separately.
The pure eye also has three meanings:
First, the sense of thorough penetration: this refers to how those three dharmas are free from marks and equal, thereby penetrating the true source.
Second, the sense of illuminating: this is a metaphor for how those three dharmas clearly understand and fully comprehend all dharma-gates.

The meaning of the three phenomena is illustrated by the way those three dharmas mutually reflect one another, as well as by the sovereign nature of the dependent origination in which all dharmas interpenetrate without obstruction.
Because these three possess such distinct and superior meanings, they are established separately under these names and are not termed "introductions."
"Category" (*pin*) means "kind" (*lei*).
Another interpretation regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) states:
before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, there was no virtuous guide, and thus [sentient beings] were like the blind.
The Buddha has now newly appeared in the world; as the Eye of the World has manifested, he is called the Pure Eye of the World.
Therefore, when the Buddha enters nirvana, it is said that the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
The remainder is as explained above.
Regarding the third point, the clarification of the fundamental tenets (*abhiprāya*), there are two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific.
Regarding the "General" [section], the patriarchs of antiquity differed in their selection of the primary tenet (*zong*).
For instance, Master Huiyuan took the *Huayan Samādhi* as his tenet;
furthermore, Master Daoyan and others took the *Dharmadhātu* as their tenet, and so forth.
Now, following Master Guangtong, I take the principle of the reality of cause-and-effect and dependent origination as the central tenet.

Cause-and-effect constitutes the state, dependent origination constitutes the meaning, and the reality of principle constitutes the essence. Because cause-and-effect and the reality of principle are non-dual, this is dependent origination.
Furthermore, cause and effect pertain to phenomena (*vastu*), while dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) brings together their characteristics; in truth, it reveals their essence (*tattva*).
Within this, two gates are established:
first, that which pertains to the text.
In some cases, there is only the fruit, as in the "Inconceivable Chapter" and the "Samantabhadra Chapter," etc.
In other cases, there is only the cause, as in the chapters from the "Difficult Questions on Clarity" through the "Numerous Multitudes Chapter" and the "Universal Worthy Chapter," etc.
Sometimes both [cause and effect] are present, as in the seventh and eighth assemblies.
Sometimes neither is present, as in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature.
If one carefully examines each assembly and each chapter, and even each individual passage, one will find that all are complete with both cause and effect; this can be seen through reflection.
Second, according to the meaning:

either cause and effect are both causes, because this is based on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and thus applies throughout the entire section, as the aspect of the fruit cannot be spoken of;
or cause and effect are both fruits, because arising is non-arising and the characteristics of causality are exhausted, which refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Either they are prior or simultaneous fruits, because the cause is that from which they arise;
or they are subsequent or simultaneous causes, because it is their fundamental basis. This is because the principle of dependent origination is thus established in reality.

Or, cause is identical to effect and effect is identical to cause; cause is not effect and effect is not cause; cause is cause and effect is effect; cause is not cause and effect is not effect—in this way, there is no obstruction and no hindrance.
Persons, dharmas, teachings, meanings, and so forth, should all be understood according to this principle.
In the subsequent detailed analysis, there are five pairs of ten phrases.
First, the pair of object and practice.
Taking the objective realm as the primary principle and practice as the goal;
or conversely, taking the cultivation [of wisdom] as the means to give rise to knowledge, thereby realizing union with the true realm.
Question:
What is the distinction between the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the goal (*abhiprāya*)? Answer:
That which is expressed by words is called the thesis; that to which the thesis leads is termed the goal.
In general, the "thesis" (*zong*) is the destination (*qu*), and this section provides the distinction between them.
Second, regarding the relative relationship between phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*):
taking phenomena as the thesis and principle as the destination.
Alternatively, it may be reversed, because the fact that dependent origination is established relies upon the principle.
Third, the relationship between teaching and meaning:
the teaching constitutes the thesis, while the meaning constitutes the objective.
Alternatively, it may be the reverse of the above, because the meaning is profound and causes the teaching to be realized.
Fourth, the relative nature of cause and fruit: the cause is the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the fruit is the goal (*yāna*).
Alternatively, it may be the opposite, because the intention to establish the fruit is taken as the cause.
This concerns the five types of persons and their respective dharmas.
Gathering the multitude constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*); preaching the Dharma constitutes the purpose (*prayojana*).
Alternatively, this is the reverse of the above, because the person is established by means of the Dharma.
In the fourth [section], when explaining the time and place of the sutra, the time is clarified first and the place is revealed afterward.
Within the section on time, four gates are established:
There are four points: first, the determination of limits; second, the inclusion of what precedes and follows; third, the manifestation of distinctions; and fourth, the indication of the Dharma.

Regarding the first, the determination of limits, Bodhiruci stated: "Among the eight assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*, the first five assemblies were taught during the initial seven days after the Buddha attained enlightenment; the sixth assembly and those following were taught during the second seven-day period, because the beginning of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states it was the 'second seven-day period.'"

Furthermore, some say that the eighth assembly was spoken at a later time, because within that text there are Śāriputra and the other five hundred śrāvakas, all of whom were converted at a later time.
These judgments likely do not accord with the text, because it is certain that no Dharma was taught during the first seven days.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason was nothing taught during the first seven days?"
"Because one practices by reflecting upon the conditions of practice.
Since it says "reflecting," it is clearly known that this does not refer to the teaching of the Dharma.
Suppose there is a rebuttal that says:
If one merely states that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are not taught while failing to state that other dharmas are also not taught, then it cannot be said that there is contemplation (*manasikāra*).
The subsequent treatise further explains: "It is for the sake of manifesting the joy in one's own dharma that [other teachings] are not spoken."
Thus, we know that the first seven days were certainly not for preaching.
Furthermore, the eighth assembly was also not at a later time.
How could it be that within a single sutra, half was preached first, other sutras were preached in the middle, and only then was it resumed again at the end?
How could it be that the Buddha lacks the power of *dhāraṇī*, such that he cannot expound all dharmas in a single thought-moment?
Jeta Grove and Śāriputra both involve the mutual interpenetration of nine periods of time; as the subsequent text states: "All past kalpas are placed within the future and the present."
"May all kalpas of the future be placed within the past.
It further says, "Within a single thought-moment, establish all the Buddha-activities of the three periods of time," and so on,
as explained at length.
Passages such as these appear everywhere [in the scriptures].
How could Śāriputra at the Jeta Grove not belong to this same category?
Thus we know that this sutra was certainly preached during the second seven-day period.
Regarding the second point, the subsumption of the preceding and succeeding [sections], there are three layers:
first, during these two periods of seven [days], one should understand that the eight assemblies were taught simultaneously.
If this is so, why would there be a sequence of before and after?
This means that, just as with the impression of a seal, when one reads it, the preceding and following parts of the text and the paper upon which the seal is made are simultaneous.
Question:
If this is so, how can the re-encounter [of the object and consciousness] be established?
Answer:
The heavy [elements] are also simultaneous because they are unimpeded, like the mutual penetration of lamp-light and so forth.
Other cases, such as remaining motionless while ascending to heaven, may be understood by applying this same explanation.
Second, at this very moment, it encompasses all immeasurable eons of the past and future without exception, because this is the time of inconceivable liberation.
Third, it encompasses infinitely nested eons and thoughts, because they are gathered and contained within one another like Indra’s net.

Third, regarding the distinction [of the teaching]: according to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, during the second seven-day period at the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times for those five persons; this is exclusively the Hīnayāna.

According to the *Guhyakapada-sūtra*, during the second seven-day period at the Deer Park, he turned the wheel of Dharma for an immeasurable multitude of beings; at that time, there were those who attained the path of Arhatship, the path of Pratyekabuddhahood, and the path of Bodhisattvahood—these constitute the Three Vehicles.

According to this sutra, during the second seven-day period, beneath the King of Trees, he turned the inexhaustible wheel of Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas, clarifying that this is the One Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "the three above are simultaneous": with respect to the Dharma, it signifies that the fundamental and the derivative are simultaneous; with respect to persons, it reveals that the capacities and responses of beings differ.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he preached after twenty-one days; according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, after six or seven days; according to the *Udānavarga* (or *Qǐxìngxíng jīng*), after forty-nine days; according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, after fifty-six days; according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, after fifty-seven days; and according to the *Shí'èr yóu jīng*, it was only after one year that he preached.
These differences arise because the capacities of those for whom the provisional teachings were intended vary; since each requires a distinct teaching to be heard, the durations differ.
Because the capacities for the fundamental teaching are fixed, it consists of only two seven-day periods.
Regarding the fourth point, the representation of the Dharma, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The time, place, and so forth are compared and measured in order to manifest its superiority."
Because this Dharma is supreme, it is taught at the beginning and in a preeminent location.
This has three meanings:
first, at the beginning of this sutra, it indicates that the fundamental Dharma is supreme.
Second, the teaching on the branches is likewise the same, because the branches do not depart from the root;
third, it reveals that the root is not the branches, and therefore the time is fixed at two weeks, with no other explanation.
Regarding the second [section], the locations where the sutras were preached, five gates are established:

first, determining the location; second, clarifying the integration and inclusion; third, revealing the distinctions; fourth, providing a general representation of the Dharma; and fifth, specifically revealing the assemblies at each location.
Regarding the first point, the location of the teaching: Question—
Is the place where this sutra was preached a pure land,
or is it a defiled realm?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions entail errors. Why?

If this were a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*), why would the preceding passage refer to "the kingdom of Magadha," and the subsequent passage again refer to "this Jambudvīpa among the four continents" and so forth? From this, one should know that it is not a pure land.

If this were a teaching concerning the defiled land, why would the subsequent text state, "This Lotus Treasury World-Ocean shakes in six ways and eighteen modes," and so forth? It is clear from this that this sutra was not preached in a defiled land.
Since these characteristics are thus contradictory, how can they be specified?
Answer:
Relying solely on this sutra, the two lands of defilement and purity are fused and mutually inclusive, forming four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
Alternatively, it may be only the Sahā world, because one follows from the root to the branches;
or it may be only the Flower Treasury World, because one follows from the branches back to the root.
These two cases have been distinguished above.

Or they may appear as a pair, for the Sahā world exists in dependence upon the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-kṣetra*); thus, the aspects of defilement and purity are distinguished, as the derivative depends upon the fundamental.
As the subsequent text states: "Within the Flower Treasury World is the Sahā World."
This is what is meant.
Alternatively, both defilement and purity may be transcended, for the ocean of fruition is ineffable.
These four aforementioned gates constitute a single realm, which is fused and unimpeded, such that any of them may be invoked as one speaks.
Second, regarding the clarification of integration and inclusion, there are also three levels:
first, this awakening beneath the tree includes the eight assemblies among humans and devas; therefore, it is said that all are not apart from this.
Second, it encompasses all lands of the ten directions without exception, such that none are ever apart from beneath this king of trees.

Third, it encompasses the infinitely layered lands within a single mote of dust on the tip of a hair, like the net of Indra, which is inexhaustible, because they are all subsumed within this Lotus Treasury World-realm.
Third, regarding the manifestation of distinctions: there are three types of locations where the Buddha preached the sūtras.
First, the sixteen great kingdoms solely within the realm, which are the locations where the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body) taught.
This applies to both the teachings of the Hīnayāna and the Three Vehicles (Triyāna).

The second refers exclusively to the various wondrous and pure lands outside the [ordinary] realms, specifically the places where the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*) teaches within the eighteen perfect lands of enjoyment (*sambhogakāya*), as described in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other texts.
This wondrous pure land is not subsumed within the three realms, yet it is not separate from them either, because it pervades all places.
This applies to the teachings of both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.

The three—defilement, purity, and their perfect interfusion—are as inexhaustible as Indra’s net; within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), the ten Buddhas preach the Dharma, wherein the environment and its inhabitants are seamlessly integrated, encompassing the three worlds.
This is a teaching place for the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) alone.
What is being analyzed here pertains precisely to the latter one, while also subsuming the former two, because their fundamental and derivative aspects are inseparable.
Regarding the fourth point, the general indication of the Dharma: it relies upon these excellent locations (*śubha-sthāna*) to indicate the excellence of the Dharma.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because this Dharma is excellent, it is taught in excellent locations."
The exposition consists of two gates:
first, the general; second, the specific.
The general section has three layers:

First, because he attained *bodhi* beneath this tree, he does not give rise to such [contradictory] statements; it clearly demonstrates that what is taught is identical to what was realized, for there is no alteration made to suit the varying capacities of different beings, as in the case of the teaching at the Deer Park and elsewhere.
Second, by relying on the perfectly interfused Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), it signifies that what is taught is perfect and sublime, for its nature is to be in full bloom.

Third, by relying on this locus of the multilayered Indra’s Net (*indrājāla*), it signifies that what is taught is likewise multilayered and inexhaustible, such as the inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*) and so forth.
These three [categories] encompass all eight assemblies; therefore, they are called "general.
Regarding the second [category], the five specific locations and assemblies, there are two parts:
first, in terms of the Buddha responding to the capacities of sentient beings, there are eight distinct assemblies.
Second, regarding the Bodhisattva’s quest for the Dharma, there are fifty-four assemblies.
The first of these, the initial assembly, was held in the kingdom of Magadha—here translated as the "Inviolable Kingdom"—at the site of the Path of Quiescence beneath the Bodhi tree.

This first assembly site is both general and specific; it is called "general" because it penetrates through and connects with the other assemblies, as the subsequent text states: "Beneath the Bodhi tree, on the summit of Mount Sumeru," and so forth. Therefore, this initial location serves as the general site.
As stated below, in all these ten sets of phrases, the first phrase in each serves as the general heading while the remaining nine serve as the particulars; this is what is meant.
The general gate that expresses the Dharma has already been clarified as before.
To specifically indicate the teaching on the qualities of the fruit within this assembly, this place where the fruit is attained is used as a representation.
The second assembly was held in the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall in the kingdom of Magadha.

According to tradition from the Western Regions, this hall is located about two or three *li* southeast of the Bodhi tree, within a bend of the Nairañjanā River, and was constructed for the Buddha by various nāgas.

The Tathāgata emits the light of the *cakra* (wheel) mark from within it, illuminating the boundless worlds of the ten directions; therefore, this is named the Hall of Universal Light (*Puguang Fatang*).
Herein is symbolized the teaching that the practice of faith is universally pervasive, providing shelter for those of initial capacity.
The third assembly was held at the Palace of Śakra on the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the Hall of Sublime Victory (Vaijayanta).

"Sumeru" is translated here as "Wondrous High Mountain" (Miaogao Shan); it is called "wondrous" because it is composed of the four precious substances, and it is called "high" because it towers above all other mountains.

This indicates that the ten stages (daśabhūmi) described herein are non-retrogressive; they reach the summit of the mountain, transcending the ordinary and the small vehicles, as they are based upon the Sublime and Victorious.
The fourth assembly was held in the Palace of Jewel Adornments in the Yāma Heaven.
The name Yama means "Time," or alternatively, "Well-Knowing.
This signifies that the ten practices are cultivated progressively according to the seasons, and as supreme virtues mutually adorn one another, this palace is designated accordingly.
The fifth assembly was held in the Palace of Universal Jewel Adornment in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Tuṣita is translated here as "Contentment" (Santuṣṭi).
It signifies that the stage of dedicating [merit] toward the world has reached fulfillment, thereby accomplishing the practice of contentment.
It encompasses virtue and extensive learning, and is entrusted to the Palace of All Jewels.
The sixth assembly was held in the Maṇiratnagarbha Hall of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

This signifies that the *tathatā* realized through the ten stages is not something produced by oneself; furthermore, it signifies that when the causal conditions are perfected at the summit of the desire realm, the wisdom-jewel (*maṇi*) emits the light of the *āgama*. For these reasons, this hall is relied upon as the locus of the assembly.
The seventh assembly is held again in the Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguang Fantang).

This signifies that the dharma-practices of the six stages explained herein are fully encompassed and perfected based upon the preceding [stages] such as faith; therefore, the assembly is convened once more at this location.
The eighth assembly was held at the Gabled Lecture Hall in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
It was for the sake of manifesting the Dharma-gate of the Dharmadhātu revealed by the signs, which, in its essential nature, possesses marvelous efficacy in saving sentient beings.
Because it arises based on the physical body and forms successive tiers like a multi-storied pavilion, it is designated by this location.
Question:
From the human realm upward, one should next first reach the Four Heavenly Kings.
What is the specific significance of transcending that [stage] to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
Answer:
The Ten Faiths are situated within the human realm, whereas the Ten Abidings reside upon the mountain peak.
Faith is the stage of the external ordinary bodhisattva; abiding therein is the non-retrogressive worthy person (*bhadra-puruṣa*).
To manifest the vast disparity between the two positions of the worthy and the ignorant—advancement and retreat—the [text] designates this as being beyond the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Question:
Having completed the assembly in Tuṣita, one next approaches Nirmāṇarati; what further purpose is there in ascending beyond to Paranirmita-vaśavartin?
Answer:
One should dedicate [the merit] toward the Tuṣita stage; the cultivation of worldly marks has now concluded.
The practices of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven consist of ten stages, while the supramundane true suchness is what is realized here.

Since the mundane and supramundane differ, and there is a distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), and since the provisional cultivation and the true realization are vastly separated, this [stage] is shown to transcend the Nirmāṇarati heaven.
Question:
Why is it necessary to convene another assembly?
Furthermore, for what reason is this assembly convened solely at the Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā) [Buddha-land]?
Answer:

Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*) is the beginning of the arousal of faith (*śraddhotpāda*), extending through the successive stages up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Now, we clarify the practices within these stages; since the cultivation of practice begins from the outset, it is logically appropriate to converge upon this point.
First, regarding the assembly in terms of stages and characteristics: it is by means of these stages and characteristics that one understands the convergence of ascent and descent;
while practice proceeds toward the profound principle, each stage encompasses the others, and thus the assembly is held only at this location.

Second, regarding the assembly for bodhisattvas seeking the Dharma: as when the youth Sudhana, at the great stupa in the Śāla forest to the east of the city of Awakening, was first taught the Dharma by Mañjuśrī for the sake of the great multitude and Sudhana himself in a single assembly.

In this sequence, continuing until the very end, at the site of the Vajragarbha Bodhimanda, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifested for the great assembly and for Sudhana and others the Dharma of the Clouds of the Dharmadhātu-body; this constitutes the final fifty-fourth assembly, and thus, including the preceding ones, there are sixty-two assemblies in total.
This is stated according to one direction.
If we discuss the universal connection throughout the worlds of the ten directions, then these are assemblies in places equal in number to the atoms and the void of the dharma-realm.
Regarding the fifth, the definitive teaching of the Lord, this is also treated in five sections:

first, the definitive nature of the Buddha-body; second, clarifying its inclusive integration; third, revealing its distinctions; fourth, representing the Dharma; and fifth, elucidating its functional activity.
Regarding the first point, "the bodies of the Buddhas": Question:
What kind of bodies are these Buddhas of the eight assemblies?
Answer:

Some commentators explain that this is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) Buddha, because the attainment of the eightfold path beneath the Bodhi tree is the manifestation of a transformation body;
because not departing from the ascent to heaven is a further transformation;
and because Śākyamuni is named Vairocana as an alternative name, rather than being a separate *vipākakāya* (retribution body).

Furthermore, another interpretation states that the Buddha who preached this sutra is the *sambhogakāya* (recompense body), because he is the *dharmadhātu-kāya* (dharma-realm body) of Vairocana and because he dwells within the pure land of the Lotus Treasury.
In the first part of the seventh assembly below, there is a praise of the Buddha’s twenty-one kinds of sublime merits, which constitute his true retribution-body (*vipākakāya*);
yet because this does not exclude the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it encompasses this scene beneath the tree, though it is not the transformation-body itself.

Now, regarding this Buddha, according to the subsequent text, he is the body of these ten Buddhas who pervade the three worlds; for it is taught that what is seen prior to the stages—such as the ten levels of faith and the three stages of the worthy and noble—is not the true retribution-body.

However, because dwelling in the Flower Treasury (*puṣpakaraṇḍa*) is not a transformation body, and because the lands, bodies, and so forth are not like the former two [the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*], they fully encompass the former two through the mutual interpenetration of their nature.
Being complete with primary and attendant manifestations like a net of Indra (*indrājāla*), these are exclusively the ten Buddha-bodies that pervade the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Second, regarding the comprehensive integration, there are two points:
first, it directly integrates all three worlds exhaustively, because only by possessing these three matters does one become a Buddha.
The three bodies and the two bodies are merely subsumed within the "wisdom of perfect enlightenment" among these three.
All wondrous pure lands and the bodies born therein are entirely subsumed within this.

Second, within the pores of the primary reward-body and the atoms of the environmental reward, all things are infinitely and perfectly complete; they subsume all phenomena of the three worlds and so forth, appearing like the Indra’s net. This can be understood by applying the same principle of reflection.

Third, regarding the manifestation of distinctions: this single body of Śākyamuni appears in various forms according to the diverse capacities of sentient beings. Sometimes he appears as an ordinary being rather than a sage, such as when he is seen with the body and feet of a three-footed black elephant or in the form of a tree spirit; these instances pertain to the realms of humans and devas.
Alternatively, he is a sage but not an ordinary person, because he shares the same physical body as an arhat-sage.

Alternatively, he is both ordinary and a sage, because he possesses a true retribution body born of father and mother, which is composed of the four great elements and thus shares the nature of an ordinary person's body.
One who possesses the fivefold Dharma-body and has exhausted all outflows (āsrava) is a sage (ārya).
Alternatively, one may be neither ordinary nor a sage, because such a person is subsumed within the three bodies (trikāya) of the Mahāyāna, and thus differs from the sages of the Hīnayāna arhats.

Alternatively, it may be a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) that is not a retribution-body (vipākakāya), because it manifests the eight signs [of a Buddha] within Jambudvīpa; yet, as distinct from the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), it is established as a true retribution-body, as taught in texts such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*. This explanation pertains to the Initial Teaching (ādikarmika-yāna).

Alternatively, it is the retribution for the transformation through non-Dharma; that is, this very body possesses twenty-one kinds of sublime qualities because it is a body of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*), as stated at the beginning of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*. This refers to the Final Teaching (*paryantavāda*).
Alternatively, there are dharmas that are neither retribution nor transformation, because form is itself suchness (*tathatā*). As the Sūtra says: "This body of mine is now the Dharma-body.
This refers to the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*).
Alternatively, it is both Dharma-body and both Reward and Transformation-bodies, as previously stated in the threefold explanation.

Alternatively, it is neither Dharma-body nor Reward and Transformation-bodies, because these are the ten Buddhas, because they pervade the three worlds, and because they are complete with their primary figures and attendants; this is as explained in the later sections of this sutra, which refers here to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Therefore, this body of Śākyamuni is perfectly interfused and unimpeded, making it extremely difficult to conceive.
Fourth, as for the representation of the Dharma: there are, in total, four types of Buddhas who preach the Dharma.
The first is the Buddha in the form of an Arhat, which represents the preaching of the Hīnayāna.
Second, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha represents the teaching of the Three Vehicles, explaining extensively that which precedes the stages and briefly that which pertains to the stages.
Third, the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha represents the teaching of the Three Vehicles, explaining extensively that which pertains to the stages and briefly that which precedes the stages.
The forty bodies of the Buddha represent the One Vehicle, wherein the six stages are taught simultaneously.
Because that which is taught therein possesses the inexhaustible dharma of the primary and its attendants, the Buddha likewise conforms to this, possessing the inexhaustibility of the ten bodies.
Fifth, regarding the clarification of karmic function:
Question—The subsequent text states, "Without leaving the Bodhi tree, he ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," and so forth.
How is it that he attains ascent to heaven without rising?
Answer:
Some commentators explain that the original body of Śākyamuni did not leave the Bodhi tree, but instead manifested a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to ascend to heaven.
According to this view, the original body of Śākyamuni never ascended to heaven at all; the body that ascended to heaven was not the original Śākyamuni.
The intent of the sutra is not so, and thus it is untenable.
Furthermore, there is an interpretation stating that non-arising is the Dharma-body, while ascending to heaven is its transformative function (*nirmāṇa*).
This is likely unreasonable; for how could the Dharma-body sit beneath the Bodhi tree?
Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states: this ascent to heaven is "reaching without going," because that which has already gone is not "going.
For this reason, it does not arise. Because "not going" is itself "going," one ascends to heaven.
For instance, the phrase "coming with the characteristic of not coming" refers to [the Buddha] being "welcomed with a 'Welcome'" (*svāgata*) and so forth.

If one relies on this interpretation, it merely means that he ascends to heaven without the characteristic of ascending; it does not mean that there was a non-arising body beneath the tree. Therefore, this [interpretation] is also difficult to employ.
Now, in explaining this passage, there are briefly eight meanings.
First, regarding the location, it refers to the entrance-gate.

This means that because all locations are contained within a single location, these celestial palaces and so forth have been inherently present beneath that king of trees; therefore, it is said that they do not "arise."
However, since this celestial palace had not previously been used, and because it is now intended to be used for the purpose of preaching the Dharma therein, it is said that he "ascends.
Furthermore, because their characteristics are identical, there is no distinction between the gate and its arising; thus, there is an ascent.
Second, with respect to the Buddha:

this body of the Buddha sitting beneath the King of Trees (Bodhi tree) is itself omnipresent throughout all places of the Dharma-realm; therefore, the Buddha-body has always been present in such places as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and thus does not need to arise from elsewhere.
Now, because one intends to employ this Buddha within the gate of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it is called "ascending.
Therefore, if he were to arise [from his seat], it would not constitute an ascent.
Third, the restriction by time.
This means that by virtue of the Buddha’s body beneath this tree, he pervades all nine periods of time—past, present, and future—as well as the tenth period, which encompasses all time.

Therefore, whether this Buddha is sitting beneath the tree, ascending to heaven, or arriving at his celestial abode, at each and every moment he pervades the entire Dharma-realm and exhaustively encompasses the limits of past and future. Thus, one knows that the time he sits beneath the tree is forever without a time of arising; hence, it is said that he "does not arise."

If it is also thus when in the very act of going, then there is only going and nothing else; in every moment they do not reach one another, yet each gathers the entire dharma-realm. Such is the gate of dependent origination: unimpeded and eternally inseparable.
Fourth, regarding the gate of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*):
because this ascending departure lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it subsumes the true suchness dharma-realm (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*).
Since sitting beneath that tree and so forth are likewise not different from suchness, they are identical to true suchness.
Because it manifests through the gate of departure, one ascends without rising.
Fifth is the analysis according to the gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
that is to say, sitting occurs because of walking; sitting exists within walking.
Walking proceeds by means of sitting, for walking exists within sitting.
Therefore, because one sits while walking, one ascends to heaven without rising; because one walks while sitting, one ascends to heaven without rising.
Because walking and sitting are without obstruction, one ascends while sitting and sits while constantly ascending.
Sixth, this concerns the inconceivable virtues of the Buddha.

That is to say, without even rising from this seat, he is simultaneously walking, lying down, standing, reaching all places, and performing all activities; none of these are known by those of the lower stages.
Seventh, in terms of what is symbolized:
it signifies that the practices of the preceding stage have been perfected, reaching ultimate firmness and indestructibility; thus it is said that he "does not rise from his previous seat.
Yet, because he possesses the function of responding to sentient beings' capacities, it is said that he "ascends."
Eighth, regarding the formation of assemblies:
this means that a subsequent assembly must necessarily include the preceding one; therefore, one does not abandon the former to form the latter.
If one were to abandon the former, it would destroy dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); for this reason, one does not arise from the former to ascend to the latter.
The sixth section concerns the distinctions among the categories of assemblies (*gaṇa*), which is divided into ten gates:

first, clarifying the number of assemblies; second, the new and the old; third, the determination of the vessels; fourth, the mundane and the supramundane; fifth, the realms and destinies; sixth, the various vehicles (*yāna*); seventh, the provisional and the real; eighth, the stages and grounds; ninth, the symbolic dharmas; and tenth, cause and effect.

Regarding the number of assemblies at the beginning: it is said that this first assembly consists of fifty-five groups. From Samantabhadra down to the Maheśvara assembly constitutes thirty-four groups; from Sudharmasāgara back to Samantabhadra constitutes eighteen groups; when added to the previous total, they comprise fifty-two assemblies.
The inner assembly of Sāgaramati, together with those newly gathered from the ten directions and the assembly of Jinaśvara, when added to the preceding, constitute fifty-five assemblies in total.
In the second assembly, there are both new and old groups; when added to the preceding, they constitute fifty-seven assemblies in total.
The second and third assemblies each have two groups—the celestial kings and the bodhisattvas; added to the previous [groups], they total sixty-one groups.
Within the "Ascent to Heaven" chapter of the fifth assembly, there are fifty-two groups, plus the gathered multitude; added to the previous [groups], they total one hundred and fourteen groups.

In the sixth assembly, there are two groups—the co-arisen and the ordinary beings—and with the single group of the seventh assembly added to the previous total, there are one hundred and seventeen assemblies in all.
In the eighth assembly, there are three groups—the bodhisattvas, the śrāvakas, and the celestial kings—which, when added to the previous [groups], constitute one hundred and twenty assemblies.
Within these, each individual group may be measured by the number of atoms in ten buddha-worlds; such as these are all without limit.

This, however, is spoken merely with reference to the eight assemblies within this single world-system; if one were to encompass all worlds throughout the ten directions, the void, and the dharma-realm, each possessing its own boundless assemblies, interpenetrating one another in infinite layers like a celestial net, then it would be "unspeakably unspeakable."
This is called the assembly of the Flower Adornment Ocean.
Regarding the second point, concerning the new and old assemblies within the various gatherings: in some cases there are only old assemblies and no new ones, such as the second and sixth assemblies;
in other cases there are only new assemblies and no old ones, such as the third, fourth, fifth, and seventh assemblies.
Some assemblies are both new and old, such as the first two and the third assembly of the eight assemblies.
The remaining intentions are each explained below in the section on the gathering of the assembly.
Regarding the three types of fixed vessels, in general discussion there are three meanings for enumerating the assembly:
First is the direct response (*dangji*), second is the indirect influence (*yingxiang*), and third is the provisional teaching (*jifa*); the present case encompasses all three.
Regarding the fourfold classification of mundane and supramundane, there are four interpretations:
first, both may be mundane, because they manifest within time and because they are one among the three mundane worlds.
Alternatively, all of these are supramundane, because their practices and virtues are not subsumed under the mundane.
Alternatively, they are both mundane and supramundane, because they possess the characteristics of both.
Furthermore, according to the *Anulakṣaṇa-śāstra*, the first [category], such as Samantabhadra and others, is supramundane, while the remainder are mundane.
Or it is neither mundane nor supramundane, because it is comprised by both the mundane-supramundane and the supramundane.
Therefore, this assembly encompasses these three positions and possesses these four propositions.

Regarding the five realms of rebirth (*gati*), among the three realms (*dhātu*), the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) are excluded because their provisional designations (*prajñapti*) based on characteristics are not particularly distinguished;
however, according to the *Rājarṣi-sūtra*, the formless heavens and so forth are also included.
Among the five destinies, the assembly of hell-beings is excluded because their suffering is so extreme that even representing the Dharma through their characteristics would not be superior;
however, in the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, this assembly is also present.
Furthermore, there is no separate assembly of human kings, because their characteristics are not distinct from those already mentioned.
Alternatively, the bodhisattvas themselves constitute the human assembly.
Or, as explained regarding the eighteen assemblies later on, only the assembly of kings is listed to signify mastery over the Dharma.
Alternatively, it may include both kings and ministers, as stated in the account of the thirty-four assemblies, because it comprises both the principal figures and their retinues.
Regarding the six vehicles, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If it is a sūtra of the Hīnayāna, only the assembly of śrāvakas is listed at the beginning."
If, at the beginning of a Mahāyāna sūtra, both the bodhisattva and śrāvaka assemblies are fully enumerated,
then by analogy, if it is a sūtra of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), only the bodhisattvas are enumerated at the outset.
How is this known?

That treatise designates the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others as "common teachings," while specifically designating the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as the "uncommon teaching," because it was not taught in common with the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, each of these three preceding sections contains two explanations.

Regarding the first two: first, if one seeks to establish the attainment of the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and so forth, one lists only the Śrāvakas; this refers to the "foolish Dharma" Hīnayāna, as taught in scriptures such as the *Āgamas*.

The second is for the purpose of turning [practitioners] away from the Hīnayāna and clarifying the intended audience; by listing only the Śrāvakas, it is shown to be a Mahāyāna teaching for those who have turned their minds [from the Lesser Vehicle], as explained at the beginning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The second [category], that which possesses both within the two assemblies, also has two types:
first, listing the śrāvakas first and the bodhisattvas later; this applies to all three teachings—gradual, sudden, and perfect—as explained in such scriptures as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Second, there are cases where bodhisattvas are listed first and śrāvakas are listed afterward; this applies to both the sudden teaching (dun-jiao) and the shared teaching (tong-jiao), as distinguished in such texts as the *Rāmaka-sūtra*, the *Vairocana-rāja-sūtra*, and the *Huixiu-sūtra*.
The third category lists only Bodhisattvas; within this, there are two types:

first, those that list Bodhisattvas but lack both principal and attendant figures, which belong to the *samvṛti-yāna* (provisional One Vehicle), as explained in texts such as the *Ekādaśamukha-sūtra*.
Second, if both the principal and its attendants are fully present, this refers to the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle, as explained in this sutra.

Regarding the seventh point, the provisional and the real: if we consider the three vehicles, when the Buddha dwells in this Sahā world, the diverse assembly is "real" because they are born through the retribution of reality;
the bodhisattvas are "provisional" because they manifest through skillful means, as the sutra says: "Those bodhisattvas conceal their immeasurable powers of mastery," and so forth.
Alternatively, the bodhisattvas may be real, because bodhisattvas prior to the stages still arise in this land;
whereas the mixed assembly may be provisional, for according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, they are all manifested through the provisional forms of great bodhisattvas from other lands.
If the Buddha dwells in a pure land, the bodhisattvas are exclusively real, because they are born through the retribution of reality;

the diverse assembly consists of emanations, for they do not exist as substantial realities. As the treatise states: "In the land of enjoyment, there are in fact no such sentient beings; however, in order to ensure that the pure land is not empty, he manifests such diverse classes of beings through transformation."

If, within the One Vehicle, the Buddha resides here in this Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbhadhatu), and both the bodhisattvas and the miscellaneous assembly are entirely real, it is because they are manifested through the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) and are comprised of actual virtues;
or, if both are entirely provisional, it is because they appear in accordance with conditions.
Other meanings should be inferred accordingly.
Eighth, clarifying their stages: if categorized according to the Three Vehicles, these such as Samantabhadra are all Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage or above.
Since those spirit-kings are for the most part comprised within the "births that accord with [the beings they assist]," they are of the eighth stage or above.

If, within the One Vehicle, all stages are equal in accordance with the limit of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), then a single person possesses all five stages; by this principle, each stage is understood to be universally inclusive.
Regarding the "Dharma of the Nine Persons": within the Three Vehicles, these persons are merely used as a medium to manifest the Dharma; thus, the persons themselves are not the Dharma.
Within the One Vehicle, however, all such persons are dharma-gates of the dependent origination of the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, this single assembly also encompasses the three worlds, as some manifest with bodies that are lands such as rivers, ponds, wells, or springs.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the ten aspects of cause and effect: if one considers the Three Vehicles, they consist solely of the stage of the cause.
If, within the One Vehicle, all are causes because they have not yet attained Buddhahood;
or if all are fruits because they appear together within the Ocean-Seal of the Buddhas, and furthermore, because they enter the ocean of the Buddhas through the power of the vehicle’s liberation.
Alternatively, it may encompass both cause and effect due to the two preceding meanings;
or it may be neither, because it is equal by virtue of being free from intrinsic nature.
These points are all distinguished in the subsequent section on "Praising Qualities."
Regarding the seventh section, "The Questions of the Various Assemblies," there are four gates:
first, clarifying existence and non-existence; second, revealing the dharmas inquired about; third, identifying the persons who inquire; and fourth, the ritual of questioning.

Regarding the presence or absence of inquiries at the beginning: among the eight assemblies, there are inquiries at the first and second [assemblies] and at the last two; they are absent in all other assemblies.

The reason for this is that in the first assembly, there is an inquiry because it establishes the cause for attaining the fruit; in the second assembly, there is an inquiry because it seeks the cause in order to reach the fruit.
However, because there are gradations in rank among the stages within the causal path, the answers are provided across five assemblies;
since there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority at the level of fruition, the answer is given in a single assembly.
